Melania Trump brokers a ceasefire deal in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city to get relief aid in
articles.description: Melania Trump brokers a ceasefire deal in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city to get relief aid in AP News Russia, Ukraine agree on ceasefire in embattled town, to hold peace talks next month Reuters Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis The Guardian US Says Russia, Ukraine to Let Civilians Leave War-Torn Oleshky Bloomberg Melania Trump brokered ceasefire at besieged Uk
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump has brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can be delivered and civilians can be evacuated from a place she said is “on the brink of disaster.” The localized ceasefire is set to begin next week. Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian relief to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine. Melania Trump, who worked with officials from both countries on a separate matter, initiated talks about Oleshky after learning about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said in announcing her involvement. She and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire, the White House said. Ukraine’s top negotiator in the effort told The Associated Press that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday — two days before the mission begins — and last several days. Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions. Russian officials also confirmed the agreement. Lubinets earlier Friday thanked Melania Trump and said the deal would be tough to accomplish. He said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online. “The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed the first lady’s announcement. Through spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric, Guterres said he hopes the local pause in fighting can become a step toward “an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire” leading to “a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine in line with international law.” Lubinets said the operation would involve removing mines on the way to Oleshky before the physical delivery of humanitarian supplies and the arranging of evacuations. He gave no further details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or implemented, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to comment when asked if Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine. “When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination,” he said. “For several weeks, we discussed many questions, initiatives and ideas. We established new approaches, mechanisms and tools to do everything possible to help civilians in Oleshky survive.” The White House announced first lady Melania Trump has brokered an upcoming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the war-ravaged Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians. As President Donald Trump departed the White House he was asked if she would be part of trilateral negotiations. Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday in Moscow — or late Monday in the United States — “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.” Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said. Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on “organizing a humanitarian mission” in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia’s priority. The first step will be to clarify what people need and organize the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the first lady. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort. Peskov said “those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether they would be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days. Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote to Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman. “What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president told reporters at the White House. The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system. Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia. Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place. He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin. Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead. Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed. Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive. Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington, Volodymyr Yurchuk, Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Edith Lederer in New York contributed to this report.

Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
articles.description: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran AP News Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change The Guardian In Florida, Trump vows to deal with Cuba after Iran gets settled Reuters Rubio urges Cubans to work with CIA to bring political change to communist-run island Fox News Cuba mocks US 'desperation' calling on Cubans to work with CIA Le Monde.f
articles.content: FORT MYERS, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country. Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries. “We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.” Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened. In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.” Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government. Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.” Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity. “The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation. “We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.” Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the U.S. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government. During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership — was “deep into negotiations with Cuba,” saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.” Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal,” adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.” Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana. Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States. Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C., and can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP. AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed from Washington.

articles.title: Mount Clemens company ‘crushed’ about employee killed in explosion
articles.content: State officials investigating an explosion at a Mount Clemens scrapyard that resulted in a fatality have released preliminary information on the victim’s death. Meanwhile, the scale buyer who was killed at Basic Metals Inc. has been identified by the Macomb County Sheriff’s Office as Christopher Cholewa, 49, of Macomb Township. The Michigan Occupational Safety and Health Administration (MiOSHA) said Friday that Cholewa was “using a grinder to cut a compressed natural gas cylinder when it exploded.” The agency listed his age as 48. Cholewa was employed as a scale buyer, or someone who weighs materials at scrap yards or recycling centers, officials said. Also Friday, Basic Metals released a photograph of Cholewa and a statement about the loss, saying the company is “crushed” by the loss. The statement appears to have been at least partially written by Cholewa’s brother-in-law. “Yesterday, tragedy struck the Basic Metals family. An accident claimed the life of long-term beloved teammate, Chris,” says the statement on the company’s Facebook page. “We are crushed. I am crushed. Knowing he won’t ever be there in the morning opening the gates, or at the scale lifting things with ease that would take two of me to do … it’s impossible to wrap our heads around. And yet, I haven’t stopped thinking about that since the moment it happened. “No one has ever been more beloved by our customers, the employees – everyone – than Chris … and for me, the guy behind the keyboard, personally – he was my brother. Uncle to my children, husband to my sister, and ‘favorite child’ to my Mother. The best person I ever knew. The type of man everyone that met him wished they could be more like. “From Basic — condolences to the family, the friends, the customers, our employees – everyone who will miss him.” Ross Rohrig replied to the statement: “Anyone that dealt with Chris over the years, knows how much the positive attitude of an employee at the scrap yard can change your mood, or how well your day is going. RIP, I appreciate our encounters so much.” The blast took place about 11:35 a.m. at Basic Metals on Mary Street, between Cass Avenue and Hubbard Street. Merchants at nearby businesses said the explosion was extremely loud. Dozens of first responders arrived at the scene, including the Macomb County Sheriff’s Office and the Mount Clemens Fire Department. The sheriff’s office said the victim was transported to McLaren Macomb hospital in Mount Clemens, where he was pronounced deceased. The incident is being investigated by the Sheriff’s Office and the MiOSHA, officials said. Basic Metals is a full-service industrial recycling company that specializes in production scrap and commercial cleanouts, according to the company’s website. Macomb Daily Staff Writer Mitch Hotts contributed to this report

articles.title: Department of Justice to send election monitors to East Lansing again on Election Day
articles.description: For the second election this year, the U.S. Department of Justice is planning on sending election monitors to East Lansing, the Michigan Attorney General’s Office said in a news release Thursday. Along with six other Michigan municipalities, the state attorney general’s office said President Donald Trump’s administration informed East Lansing that it will be sending...
articles.content: For the second election this year, the U.S. Department of Justice is planning on sending election monitors to East Lansing, the Michigan Attorney General’s Office said in a news release Thursday. Along with six other Michigan municipalities, the state attorney general’s office said President Donald Trump’s administration informed East Lansing that it will be sending federal monitors to polling locations during the Nov. 3 election, after doing so during the August Primary. “The law provides specific parameters that allow monitors, observers and challengers to witness elections at local polling places,” Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said in the Thursday news release. “It’s important for residents to know that DOJ monitors are a standard part of our election process, and we anticipate they will comport with state and federal law just as they did in this year’s August Primary.” Back in August, East Lansing Info witnessed these election monitors at precincts around the city and heard from precinct chairs that they complied with rules, were not disruptive to election processes and were friendly towards election workers. Still, Nessel said in her news release that her office is ready to hold accountable those who would interfere with Michiganders’ ability to cast their vote. Back in June, ahead of the primary, the Trump administration sent letters to Lansing, Detroit and East Lansing, all strong Democratic voter blocks, alerting them that it would send election monitors for the primary. This was while Michiganders, amongst other races, determined which Democrats would face off in November against unopposed Republican candidates for U.S. Senate and Michigan’s 7th U.S. Congressional District. As far as the Trump administration’s rationale for monitoring those specific municipalities in August, state and local officials issued statements refuting various false claims from the Department of Justice. Some East Lansing officials had theories on unspoken reasons East Lansing could have been chosen for monitoring. East Lansing City Councilmember Mark Meadows told ELi that the Trump administration could be trying to punish the city for retaining its sanctuary city status, while former City Clerk Marie Wicks said the administration could be interested in discouraging students from voting. articles.title: Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, Senatobia mayor says
articles.description: Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, Senatobia mayor says AP News Bodycam clip released in fatal police shooting of Mississippi one-year-old BBC Officer who shot and killed Black toddler in Mississippi resigns from police force The Guardian What we know about the Senatobia officer who fatally shot Kohen Wiley localmemphis.com Mississippi releases video showing fatal police sh
articles.content: The police officer who shot and killed a 1-year-old boy in Mississippi when he fired into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call has resigned, the Senatobia mayor told The Associated Press Friday. Sgt. Hunter Foster, 33, had been cleared of criminal wrongdoing by the Mississippi Attorney General’s office earlier this week after its monthslong probe concluded his use of force had been justified. On Thursday, the state released videos of the fatal shooting of Kohen Wiley, including Foster’s body-worn camera footage of the June 14 encounter in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia, about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis, Tennessee. Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed Foster’s resignation Friday. Foster’s attorney Martin Zummach declined to comment when reached Friday. Zummach has said Foster had ‘no choice’ but to fire his weapon at the vehicle because it was moving at him. Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, has disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Ben Crump, an attorney for Kohen’s family, said the footage shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family concluded the same. An image of the vehicle shows its shattered right front passenger window. The family’s legal team called for the federal government to investigate the shooting. “Officer Foster’s resignation is hardly a step toward accountability, and it is certainly not justice,” Crump said in a statement. “Turning in a badge does not erase responsibility for taking a life, and it will not end our fight for justice for Kohen and his family.” The family’s legal team has called for Foster to be decertified as a police officer so that he cannot be hired by another law enforcement agency. Mississippi Department of Public Safety spokesperson Alex Gibert said Friday that Foster remained certified as a police officer. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday in early November. The group of officers were at the Walmart store in response to an unrelated incident, according to a Mississippi Bureau of Investigation report. A Walmart employee then alerted them of two women running from the store. The videos show Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen as she and her friend run across the parking lot and enter their vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop. The vehicle then accelerates forward as Foster steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother’s lap. The car continues to drive away. Vellesiya Wiley has denied that she and her friend stole diapers from the store and they have not been charged, according to state and county court records. Foster has worked for two other agencies in Mississippi since 2019 after becoming certified as a law enforcement officer there. He worked for the police department in Southaven, a city in DeSoto County that’s part of the greater Memphis area, for two years and then was employed with the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office until October 2024. About five months later, he was hired by the police department in Senatobia, a city of about 8,000, according to state records obtained by the AP. A lawsuit filed in federal court in Mississippi in 2021 accused Foster and a group of 12 other Southaven police officers of civil rights violations during a 2019 arrest of two Black men outside a Waffle House. The two men said they had been searching for a lost set of keys when they were violently arrested and beaten by several officers. They alleged that Foster submitted a report falsely stating that they tried to run over another officer with their vehicle. Foster and the other officers denied wrongdoing. The Southaven police department agreed to settle the case in 2022 for an undisclosed amount, court records show. Last month, Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford was fired by the city’s board of aldermen, after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged he used racist slurs in private text messages.

articles.title: From tariffs to data centers, Michigan’s big economic stories | Marketplace Morning Report
articles.description: Marketplace's Kimberly Adams speaks to Metro host Robyn Vincent about tariffs on Canada and data centers in Michigan as a part of the Economic Pulse series. The post From tariffs to data centers, Michigan’s big economic stories | Marketplace Morning Report appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Marketplace’s Kimberly Adams speaks to Metro host Robyn Vincent about tariffs on Canada and data centers in Michigan as a part of the Economic Pulse series. This interview originally aired on “Marketplace Morning Report” on Oct. 23. Listen to the “Marketplace Morning Report” each weekday at 6:51 a.m., 7:51 a.m. and 8:51 a.m. on WDET. As part of our Economic Pulse series, “Marketplace Morning Report” checks in with journalists from local public media outlets across the country to hear about the economic stories they’re following in their communities and states. This week, “Marketplace Morning Report” host Kimberly Adams spoke with Robyn Vincent. She’s the host and producer on WDET’s “The Metro” in Detroit. She came on the program to discuss how the trade war with Canada is impacting the Michigan economy — plus some fights over data centers and high utility bills in the state. The following is an edited transcript of Kimberly and Robyn’s conversation. Kimberly Adams: So, tariffs are a huge story where you are in Detroit. The Trump administration has imposed 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods. You have so much commerce back and forth across the border there in Michigan. How have these tariffs affected the Michigan economy? Robyn Vincent: Yeah, Kimberly, Michigan is hit harder than most states, and the short answer to why that is is that we’re on both ends of this. So, Michigan buys more auto parts from Canada than any other state and ships them more than any other state. So, we get taxed coming and going. I spoke with Jason Miller, who studies supply chains at Michigan State University, and he told me so far, it’s showing up in jobs more than in prices. He said importers have absorbed most of the tariffs rather than raise prices, but Michigan has lost about 4,000 jobs when it comes to people who are making auto parts in the last year, and that’s according to the state’s automotive dashboard. Adams: The automotive industry is not the only one feeling the pinch. There’s also the tourism industry. How has that been affected? Vincent: Yeah, I mean something you have to remember, Kimberly, is Detroit is a border town. Windsor, Ontario, sits directly across the river from downtown Detroit. In July, a new bridge opened between Detroit and Windsor. It’s the longest bridge of its kind in North America. Canada paid for nearly all of it, close to $5 billion. Now, here’s what’s very telling about that: the two countries were supposed to cut the ribbon together. Canada called that off. They held their own ceremony on their side of the river and pointed to the president’s tariff threats. A lot of Canadians are likely to not use this new bridge. Visit Detroit, the regional tourism bureau, tells me that visitation from Canada has been running about 30% below normal since 2025. But I’ve talked to local business owners who feel that number is much lower. That there are many more Canadians who are choosing not to cross over, not to spend their money in Detroit. I went to Eastern Market — that’s Detroit’s public market. It’s the place you go on a Saturday morning for fresh produce and artisanal cheeses and locally made goods like jewelry and leather handbags. Vendors there tell me their Canadian regulars have pretty much stopped coming. Adams: We’re coming up on the midterm elections. How much are the issues of trade and tariffs and its impact on Michigan coming up with these candidates as we get down to the final days before voting? Vincent: Yeah, they’re talking about it a lot. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed calls the president’s approach “chaotic,” “ham-fisted,” “self-serving.” He’s got the United Auto Workers behind him. Republican Mike Rogers says he’s ready to work with the president on the tariffs, the ones that are working at least, and he says that he’s ready to push back on the ones that aren’t. They are both making their pleas to voters right now that they can make change, that they will be agents of change in this moment when so many voters are angry and want to see the tariffs and the trade war come to an end. Adams: I want to shift gears now. Data centers have become a flashpoint across the country. How is that debate playing out in Michigan? Vincent: Yeah, it’s playing out in a few different places right now. Van Buren Township, which sits about 25 miles west of Detroit, is an area with farmland, subdivisions, and industrial parks, and so Big Tech has been eyeing it. And last week, it approved a Google data center that will draw a gigawatt of electricity. That’s about what 750,000 homes use. The township and Wayne County are forgiving an estimated $125 million in local taxes over the next 12 years. Residents packed meetings for 10 months, asking the board to reject it. The township supervisor, Kevin McNamara, told my colleague Quinn Kleinfelter that he didn’t have the option to say no. Kevin McNamara: A lot of them just don’t seem to understand that data centers are legal. They say, “just say no.” You can’t just say no. If you say no, you go to court, and the court decides what to do, and they decide how to build it. And as badly as maybe I didn’t want a data center, I’m not letting a judge in downtown Detroit build our data center. We’re going to build the best damn data center we possibly can. Vincent: So that’s the argument he’s made to angry neighbors for 10 months, Kimberly. Adams: Wow. Data centers are of course connected to utility bills, and the energy prices have been a story that we’ve been covering here on “Marketplace Morning Report” pretty much nonstop. How have Michiganders been feeling the price pressures? Vincent: Yeah, utilities in Michigan are the highest in the Midwest, and in the city of Ann Arbor, there’s a ballot measure that would clear the path for the city to create its own utility. And this is in response to those high utility rates and also to frequent outages that many of us here in Michigan experience; it feels like every time the wind blows, honestly. Here’s the thing, though. The Ann Arbor City Council just drafted a resolution that opposes that ballot measure, and residents are furious about this. I mean, people were seeing this ballot measure as a blueprint, if it passes, for other cities in Michigan to take on. Adams: We are less than two weeks out from the midterm elections. Y’all have an incredibly contentious Senate race there in Michigan. Are data centers or these rising utility bills coming up on the campaign trail? Vincent: They absolutely are. I mean, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has a multi-point plan, we will say, on how he plans to deal with data centers. Republican Mike Rogers is also pushing for guardrails on data centers. I would say one of the differences, though, between the two of them, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed says he wants to see money out of politics. And one of the reasons that many people feel utility rates are so high in Michigan is because DTE Energy gives a lot of money to many politicians in Michigan, and you know we have the receipts to back that up.

articles.description: The Space 2 comes in multiple colors, including an attractive seafoam green. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currentl
articles.content: My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currently on sale at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart in all three colors for an all-time low of $106.49 ($23 off), making them even easier to recommend. [Product: Soundcore Space 2 | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GR4GR5QH?tag=theverge02-20, https://goto.walmart.com/c/482924/565706/9383?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.walmart.com%2Fip%2Fsoundcore-Space-2-Anker-Active-Noise-Cancelling-Headphones-Comfortable-Fit-50H-Playtime-LDAC-Hi-Res-Wireless-Audio-Dual-Connection-Clear-Calls-Blueto%2F20012170172, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fanker-soundcore-space-2-wireless-bluetooth-noise-cancelling-over-the-ear-headphones-with-50h-anc-playtime-and-comfort-black%2FJJ858R848C%2Fsku%2F6673211] The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. They also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to various design upgrades, while retaining many of the same features that made the Sound One sound so good for the price, including support for high-resolution LDAC audio. You also still get access to HearID 3.0, which lets you personalize the sound by listening to a series of samples and adjusting accordingly. Battery life is another welcome improvement. The Space 2 can last up to 50 hours with ANC enabled or 70 hours with it switched off, up from 40 and 55 hours, respectively, on the original. And when your battery dies, you can still use the equipped 3.5mm jack for wired listening. They’ll also automatically pause playback when you take them off, which is handy when you need to step away without losing your place in a song or podcast.

UAE diplomat running for UN chief faces questions over her country's support for Sudan rebels
articles.description: UAE diplomat running for UN chief faces questions over her country's support for Sudan rebels AP News EXCLUSIVE: Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh enters race for UN chief Reuters CIP Statement on the Selection of the Next UN Secretary-General, Opposition to Nusseibeh Candidacy Center for International Policy Hebrew-speaking UAE diplomat of Palestinian descent enters race to lead UN Ynetnews U.A.E. Diplomat Jolts De
articles.content: JERUSALEM (AP) — A female diplomat from the United Arab Emirates is the newest contender for the role of United Nations secretary-general. Lana Nusseibeh brings Palestinian roots and defense of the UAE’s historic relations with Israel to her candidacy, but she faces sharp criticism over her country’s alleged role in backing paramilitary fighters who have killed thousands in Sudan’s civil war. The Gulf nation has denied the claims. Nusseibeh, who has a master’s in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies, declared her candidacy this week in a race that had largely stalled. No woman has ever led the world body throughout its 80 years of existence. Any leader succeeding Antonio Guterres in January would inherit a U.N. weakened by harsh criticism and steep funding cuts by the Trump administration. The U.N.’s role has perhaps never been more questioned as global powers create alternative bodies of influence, wars rage, hunger grows and epidemics like Ebola pose fresh challenges every day. She will face questions from U.N. General Assembly members as part of the candidacy process on Tuesday. Nusseibeh, who was nominated this week by the UAE government and has taken a leave of absence from the foreign ministry, spent over a decade as her country’s ambassador to the U.N., from 2013 to 2024. She has been outspoken on issues including aid for Palestinians in Gaza, the historic Abraham Accord with Israel in 2020 and the role of women on the international stage. A request for an interview brought no immediate response Friday. Already, the six state members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which also includes Saudi Arabia and Qatar, have unanimously backed her. “I will bring greater urgency to the work for peace,” Nusseibeh’s statement declaring her candidacy says. “I believe deeply in this institution because of where I come from. People in my region see what diplomacy and collective action can achieve. And they feel the consequences when it fails.” Nusseibeh, born in 1978, wants to “rebuild trust” in the U.N. and says it should use “quiet diplomacy” to keep disputes from escalating. She also addresses a booming global issue, artificial intelligence, saying the U.N. should build “practical international cooperation before divisions harden, including voluntary incident reporting.” Nusseibeh, whose uncle Sari Nusseibeh is a well-known Palestinian scholar, has family roots in Jerusalem and a long interest in the region beyond Gulf affairs. She is known for her advocacy for helping to get aid to the 2 million or so Palestinians trapped in Gaza. “How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to U.N. data? Because of Lana Nusseibeh — a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them to (get stuff done). She would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” Brett McGurk, former White House envoy, said on X this week. While holding the rotating presidency of the U.N. Security Council in 2023, several months before the war in Gaza began, Nusseibeh organized a special session on Palestine. And in 2025, she openly warned that Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank would be a “red line” for the UAE. But Nusseibeh could face what some believe is a conflict of interest over Sudan. The war and the UAE’s alleged role in it has been explored by various arms of the U.N. Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE backing for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces that have been fighting Sudan’s military in the civil war that erupted in April 2023. The RSF has been accused of atrocities including the attack on the city of el-Fasher in October 2025 in which the U.N. said at least 6,000 people were killed. “The U.N. has concluded, in part based on the evidence of our lab at Yale, that the massacre has the hallmarks of genocide,” Nathaniel Raymond, executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health, told the AP. He said the el-Fasher massacre could not have happened without the UAE’s provision of drones, mercenaries to operate them and artillery and mortars used in the siege of the city. “An official of the government that did this cannot be allowed to lead the United Nations, especially when this conduct is under investigation by the ICC, a U.N. body,” Raymond said. Last year, Sudan filed a case at the top U.N. court accusing the United Arab Emirates of breaching the genocide convention by arming and funding the RSF. The UAE asserted the case was “nothing more than a cynical publicity stunt.” Nusseibeh was the UAE’s point person on Sudan, according to Justin Lynch, managing director of the Conflict Insights Group research organization. “Throughout this war, she assured other governments that the UAE was not backing the RSF, even as Washington and other capitals knew internally that it was,” he told the AP. The U.N. secretary-general’s role is to protect civilians from horrors like el-Fasher, Lynch said. “Handing the job over to the diplomat who ran cover for it would be an insult to the survivors.” Associated Press writer Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
articles.description: Last week, Starshield - the version of SpaceX's Starlink used by the Ukrainian military - was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army's interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country's energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at
articles.content: Last week, Starshield — the version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by the Ukrainian military — was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army’s interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country’s energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries. The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions between himself and President Donald Trump. The abrupt nature of the cutoff and its potentially dangerous military and humanitarian ramifications led to widespread public outcry focused both on Trump for pulling the rug out from under Ukraine and on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk for enabling him. Since then Musk and Trump have traded denials back and forth. Musk first said that SpaceX has no control over Starshield and decisions are made by the US military, while the White House denied taking action. Then reports emerged that Musk was the one who suggested the slowdown tactic to Trump, who then accepted it, followed by a further report that Musk himself unilaterally ordered the restrictions. The finger-pointing is of little interest to Ukrainians, who are focused on trying to defend their country from a brutal ongoing Russian invasion. Zelenskyy is well aware that he is being used as a scapegoat as Trump flails around attempting to blame Ukraine for the rising oil prices caused by his unpopular war with Iran. But Ukraine needs to play nice to some extent, given how dependent it is on US technologies like Starlink/Starshield that enable it to mount a defense against Russian attacks. Starlink access has been deliberately restricted there before, including in 2022, when coverage was not extended to cover a counterattack operation in Crimea. If Musk decided to pull the plug completely, the effect on Ukraine could be devastating. This amount of geopolitical power being wielded by an unelected tech oligarch is the direct result of consolidating so much of the space industry into just one company, and one man’s hands. And the scope of Musk’s control goes well beyond Ukraine. From the defense of nations to the ability of NASA to launch its astronauts into space, SpaceX has been irreplaceable — and that means Musk has the space industry in his grip. A de facto monopoly SpaceX’s recent IPO positions it as one of the most valuable companies in the world. And while the company has generated most of its recent revenue from its Starlink service, it made its name as a company that launches rockets into space. SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is the most successful rocket in history, and its “rideshare” program, which lets small satellite operators share space on a rocket, has dropped the price of launches to historic lows. This has helped organizations from small startups to university research departments launch their own satellites and has been hailed as a democratizing force in the space industry. However, that success has come at a cost, which is that SpaceX now holds all the cards when it comes to access to space. “For all intents and purposes, SpaceX has a monopoly on launch right now,” said Wendy Whitman Cobb of the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. “There are competitors out there,” she said, such as United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab, “but nobody comes even close to SpaceX in terms of frequency, mass, scale, cost. I mean, they’ve got everything in the bag.” Space economist Oğuz Karasu of the Oxford Space Initiative concurred. SpaceX doesn’t have a monopoly on launch in the legal sense, he said, but in practical terms it does. And that gives the company tremendous pull over the industry as a whole. “The rocket launch industry is around 8 percent of the entire [space] industry,” Karasu said, “but without that 8 percent, you can’t have the rest of it.” The gatekeeper for space SpaceX, which didn’t respond to a request for comment, has a tremendous advantage in providing space-based services like satellite internet. The company has been able to build out its network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites currently in low Earth orbit by launching them cheaply and efficiently using its Falcon 9 rockets. “This is almost like an antitrust issue,” said defense expert Andrew Reddie of the University of California, Berkeley. “The issue is that SpaceX launches support Starlink constellations that are owned by SpaceX. There is no incentive for a SpaceX launch to be used to provide constellations for other countries that would compete.” Interestingly, SpaceX has previously launched Amazon Kuiper (now Leo) satellites on a handful of missions — arguably as a preemptive defense against antitrust complaints. Or perhaps SpaceX is simply so confident in its position that it can afford to be magnanimous (or to flex a little on its rival) by launching a few competitor satellites. The downside of a monopoly, at least for the customer, is that eventually prices rise. SpaceX doesn’t share prices for its launches publicly, but both Whitman Cobb and Karasu say they’ve heard complaints that Falcon 9 launches are getting more expensive, particularly for low Earth orbit deployments. And the Starlink service has seen considerable increases in price since its beta launch in 2020. Of course, there are plenty of reasons for a company to increase its prices, from inflation to rising costs, but when a company has enormous market dominance (and now shareholders to please) there isn’t much incentive against raising prices to increase profits. If this business model sounds familiar, it’s because it’s one of Silicon Valley’s favorite and most destructive tactics. Uber perfected the art of predatory pricing, whereby investor cash is used to artificially lower prices so that a company can corner a market and push out competition. Then, with the monopoly safely in place, the company can jack up its prices and lower the quality of its product or service, secure in the knowledge that customers no longer have any other viable alternatives. The unseen power of space This might sound like an obscure problem, something that might make life more difficult for a few high-tech operations but has little relevance to the day-to-day lives of most people. But space infrastructure is now embedded in the mechanisms of our most essential technologies, in the form of satellite communications and GPS data. “If GPS goes down, you’re not going to be able to get gas at the gas pump, you’re not going to be able to get money out of the ATM,” said Whitman Cobb, “let alone not be able to do financial transactions or get an ambulance to the right place on time.” It’s not that space experts are realistically worried that Elon Musk is going to lose his mind and cut off Starlink access worldwide, or cause a collision that could take down GPS. It’s that the space industry is woven, unseen, into so many parts of our everyday lives that allowing one company or one person to control access to space hands them enormous power. “All of our current economic activities are based on space technologies right now,” said Karasu. “Giving this much control, or this much power, to one person is not good for society’s future.” Even huge agencies like NASA and the Space Force face risks from being too dependent on SpaceX. With the company deciding to retire its workhorse and extremely reliable Falcon 9 rocket, reportedly not taking any new missions from 2028, the Space Force is struggling to find launch options for its military satellites, and NASA now faces a potential future in which it doesn’t have access to the Crew Dragon capsule for carrying its astronauts to and from the International Space Station. History has shown the dangers of having only one launch option. After the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, which cost the lives of seven astronauts, the entire program was canceled and no humans were launched into space from the US from 2011 until 2020. That’s why NASA is continuing to support beleaguered Boeing in its slow and troubled development of the Starliner capsule, because dependence on a single launch provider means putting all of your very expensive and delicate eggs into one precarious basket. That was demonstrated in February this year, when issues with the usually rock-solid reliability of the Falcon 9 temporarily grounded it, leading to concerns that NASA’s launch of the Crew-12 mission to the space station could be delayed. This was a timely reminder that even the most impressive and reliable of technologies — and, to be clear, the Falcon 9 is both an incredible feat of engineering and outstandingly successful — can have failures or outages. NASA continues to contract with smaller companies like Rocket Lab and Blue Origin, and has repeatedly stressed its desire to have multiple commercial providers for services like transporting astronauts to the space station. “Even NASA is realizing, okay, we are putting all our bets on a single player,” said space business expert Michele Scataglini of the Oxford Space Initiative and University of Oxford. “The market needs to have more competition, otherwise it’s not a market.” Whether any of these companies will be able to catch up and provide a meaningful, affordable alternative to SpaceX remains to be seen. It will be hard for any company to keep pace with SpaceX’s sister companies developing complementary technologies as well. “The complementarity of the assets that SpaceX has built — artificial intelligence, the batteries, the launch capabilities — these are all self-reinforcing capabilities for the firm, that I would say none of the other players alone possesses,” said Scataglini. Too much power in too few hands For now, with Starlink access restored in Ukraine, the country will continue to walk the tightrope of trying to defend itself using technology it does not ultimately control. Unlike previous restrictions of Starlink usage there, which were arguably more about limiting offensive capabilities, “what seems to have been impacted in this most recent episode is Ukrainian defensive capability,” said Reddie, the defense expert. “And then you end up with all the harrowing images of apartment blocks on fire and people getting pulled out of the buildings. “And so that’s the major security challenge, that you’ve effectively got a non-state actor making decisions as if they’re a government.” Scataglini concurred, describing the events in Ukraine as a global wake-up call. “There’s a single entrepreneur that has more power than governments in deciding how strategic defense capabilities can be used,” he said. In times of stress and uncertainty — and between ever-climbing costs of living, a decimated social safety net, fears about AI coming for our jobs, and rising global populism and extremism, there’s plenty to be stressed and uncertain about — it is tempting to turn our gazes inward, to look out for our own interests and prioritize the needs of our own nations. But space does not respect national boundaries, and what happens in orbit around our planet affects us all. The risk, Scataglini said, is that “we are moving into one firm dominating the launch market and deciding who goes up, and who doesn’t. Which country has access to space, and which one does not, because not all nations around the world, especially if you think about the Global South, will have easy access to these capabilities.” Looking to the future, experts hoped that out of the brutal events in Ukraine could come more public awareness of the dangers of too much power held in too few hands. “I’m cautiously optimistic that, at least in this case in particular, it is highlighting the dangers of being reliant on a single company, a single individual,” said Whitman Cobb. “It t
